title: The barber ordained first
hookLine: the Sakyan princes ask the Buddha to ordain their barber Upali before them, so they will have to bow to him (Vinaya, Cullavagga 7)

cards: A handful of young Sakyan princes slip out of town together, dressed as if for a pleasure trip. Among them are names we know: Ananda, Anuruddha, Devadatta.
They've decided to leave home and follow their kinsman, the Buddha. And they've brought their barber, Upali, the man who has cut their hair and trimmed their beards.
At the border they take off their jewelry, wrap it in a cloth, and hand the bundle to Upali. Here, they tell him. This is enough to live on.
Go home. Upali starts back. And then he stops.

teach.h: A BUNDLE HUNG ON A TREE.
teach.b: First, Upali's choice. In the Vinaya he thinks it through on the road. The Sakyans are fierce, he reasons; if I come home with their jewels, they'll think I harmed the princes.
Then a bigger thought: if these young men are leaving home, why shouldn't I? So he hangs the bundle on a tree, for anyone who wants it, and goes back to them. Second, the princes' request.
They bring Upali to the Buddha and ask for something surprising.
Ordain the barber first, they say. We Sakyans are proud. He's served us a long time.
If he's ordained before us, we'll have to stand for him, bow to him, show him respect, and our pride will be humbled. Third, why the order matters.
In the monastic community, rank comes from when you were ordained, not from your family, so whoever goes first is senior for good.
By sending the barber ahead, the princes give away the one thing their birth always handed them: going first. And the Buddha does as they ask. Upali is ordained, then the princes.
Fourth, what it shows. The story doesn't ask the barber to rise to their level.
It asks the princes to step down to his, on purpose, before their pride can set.
And the overlooked man, sent home with a bundle of jewelry, becomes their elder.

how: In Theravada monasteries monks still sit, walk and receive offerings in order of ordination, so a monk from a poor family who was ordained earlier is senior to a later monk from a wealthy one.

games.q: you're one of the princes. you're all about to be ordained, and your barber has come with you. what do you ask the Buddha?
o: ordain us first; we're his masters.
ordain the barber first, so we must bow to him.
games.why: they ask for Upali to go first, so that their Sakyan pride will be humbled, and the Buddha does it.

practice: Think of someone whose work keeps your days running and who rarely gets noticed: the person who cleans your building, the one who cuts your hair, a relative who always does the dishes.
Hold their face in mind and let them go first in your thoughts for a minute, the way the princes let Upali go first. Notice what they actually give, then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Upali. The barber the Sakyan princes asked to have ordained before them, so their pride would have to bow to him. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali upasampada, full ordination: its order sets who is senior in the community.
